title: Affective-State Plasticity Windows: A Delivery-Timing Framework for Durable Behavior Change
content: Durable behavior change is uneven: the same intervention endures in some, dissolves in others. Maintenance accounts emphasize motives, self-regulation, resources, habits and environments, under-specifying delivery timing. I introduce affective-state plasticity windows: transient intervals of unusual modifiability in a targeted representation, opened jointly by plasticity state, lability and affect. Identical intervention delivered into an open window is predicted to update behavior more durably than outside one: the window-matching principle, integrating four literatures. I specify a candidate signature from antecedent and concurrent peripheral observables; a study calibrating the first component, reaching only the second's band, and validating the third against an external criterion; and three predictions plus a sub-prediction setting timing against habit theory's context-consistency prescription. Prediction 1 crosses lability with arousal, readiness blocked, so additivity disconfirms the conjunction; the laboratory ones name their memory class. The applied prediction, untested rather than novel, tests state-matched timing given a staged reactivation, not the conjunction, and runs only above a declared detection-accuracy bar. The program is staged; on the evidence cited that bar is unlikely to be cleared, ending the applied claim as a negative result. This is theory with testable predictions, not an efficacy claim: showing any applied method works requires dedicated study.
